en: O Lord, for that illustrious one who performs Your worship through the morning contemplation of Śaṅkara, the bathing and sprinkling [of the deity], the proper restraint [of the breath], the recollection of the twilight prayers (*sandhyā*), the cleansing that pacifies sins, the ritual attendance (*upasthāna*), the satiation (*santarpaṇa*), the worship of the door, the sacrifice, and the expulsion of obstacles that have entered the abode— for him alone are the two-fold perfections attained.

O twice-born ones, the power of the Lord is in truth one and immeasurable, yet it is auspicious and assumes many forms; under the influence of the limiting adjunct of time, they meditate upon her daily in the form of Brāhmī and others.
But here, the union of the stainless Self and Śiva is the Śaivī Sandhyā; therefore, Śiva alone, who is eternally stainless, should be meditated upon by the best of practitioners.
At dawn, I remember the Lord, who dwells within the center of the lotus of my heart; whose nature is consciousness arising from the cessation of the paths of the moon and sun;
who is the soul of the universe, the end of both being and non-being, and infinite; the one to be meditated upon by the best of sages at all times for the attainment of liberation.
At midday, I constantly meditate upon Śambhu, the Lord of the Universe, the supreme cause, immeasurable, resembling a hundred thousand moons,
ever-risen, whose nature is the sky free from illusion, and who resides within the center of the bow.
At the onset of night, I constantly meditate upon that imperishable Brahman, which resembles an ocean of nectar, the sovereign of the universe, the auspicious one abiding in the unarisen sound;
it is the nectar of awakening, devoid of instrument, cause, and effect, and has its abode in the aperture of Brahma (brahmarandhra). // JsSpst_5 //

I constantly remember that treasury of splendor, immovable and auspicious, which at midnight is always to be known by those who have cast off sense-objects and perceive the ultimate reality— as imperishable, inconceivable, beyond mental cultivation, and transcending the sphere of *unmanī*.

Meditating upon his own nature as the pure state of Sādāśiva— which pervades from the earth element up to the *granthi* (the knot) through the sequence of the *tattvas*, and which transcends the *tattva* of purified knowledge (*viśuddhavidyā*)—

and performing all the excellent rites according to the preeminent rules established in the Śaiva knowledge, he should place the individual soul within his very heart, situated between the sun, moon, fire, ether, and power.

The wise person who constantly purifies this physical body of Śiva—which is composed of impurities—by means of its extensions and its parts that pervade the five paths, and who, having adorned his body with mantras, propitiates Śiva day and night and at the twilights through worship, fire-oblations, and meditative absorption; he, by means of those [purifications], attains the state of Śiva.

This deity, who is greater than the great and subtler than the subtle, is to be known as Śiva, the omnipresent one within the body by those who fear worldly existence; he is to be meditated upon and worshipped in the center of the Śivaliṅga.

Having established within the heart-lotus— the abode of Śiva known as Manasija, which is the seat of action (kriyāpīṭha) at its pericarp— that Liṅga consisting of consciousness with a purified mind through the essence of sound (nāda),

and having duly bathed it with the nectar-like water of the Self, one should worship it further with the sandalwood paste of dispassion (vairāgya), with the eight riches, with flowers such as non-violence (ahiṃsā), and so forth.

Blessed is that pure one who worships with the incense-rite born of *prāṇāyāma*, by the offering of the lamp of consciousness, by the oblation of Soma consisting of *pratyāhāra*, by the recitation of the *suṣumṇā*, by various *dhāraṇās* within that mind, by ornaments arising from stainless *dhyāna*, and by the presentation of the sacrificial cake of equanimity.

Having satiated the fire in the sacrificial pit located at the navel with an oblation consisting of nectar flowing from the moon, that person who— by means of the flame of the resonance of the Śiva-mantra arising from the *kanda*— performs self-realization through the functional state within the all-pervading light of Śiva situated in the sky of the heart, is indeed liberated and imperishable.
When the physical basis of oneself, the ritual substances, the mantras, and the linga and so forth have been purified according to the rules,
let there be no obstacle to the worship of you for the practitioners established on the path of the Siddhānta.

I bow to the seat of Śiva, which consists of the seed-syllable of the power named Dhārikā, the bud of the infinite lotus, the state of merit, awakening, dispassion, and splendor, the four syllables in reverse order, the body, the two coverings, the lotus with its filaments and pericarp, and the assembly of the circle of powers.

The bulbous root is the earth; the stalk extends to the end of the principle of Time (kālatattva); the multitude of worlds is its thorns; the thread of existence (bhāvasūtra) is the knot upon knot; the lotus of Pure Knowledge (śuddhavidyā) has eight petals mounted by the Lords of Knowledge (vidyeśāna). // JsSpst_15 //

I bow to the Lord who resides within the *bindu*, whose form is the self-mantra contained within the heart-mantra, situated upon that excellent seat of yoga which is enriched with filaments and pericarp belonging to the powers of Vāmā and the others, and accompanied by the orbs of the Sun and the rest.

Its bulbous root (*kanda*) measures one hundred million (*koṭi*) *yojanas*; its stalk (*nāla*) extends to the end of a *parārdha*; its knot (*granthi*) is ten thousand times a *parārdha* of *koṭis*; and its lotus (*abja*) is one hundred thousand (*lakṣa*).
Its form consists of the Lord (*Īśvara*), numbering ten million; its lotus of the *arbudā* [region] consists of mantra; and that body of Sadāśiva is Śiva himself, the immeasurable.

In that [lotus], the supreme form of Bindu, consisting of medicine, ornaments, and sound, is to be meditated upon by those devoted to the mantras and tantras of Śaṅkara—the auspicious Śivā, whose limbs are knowledge and action.
Salutation to that Great Śānta Sadāśiva, who bestows all sovereignty and happiness, who is incomparable, stainless, and known as Nāda, and who is of the nature of Sadāśiva.
He should always be meditated upon as residing in the center of the circle of the sky, situated within the lotus-heart of the unobstructed, pure yogi of Śiva;

he whose body extends from the Lord (Īśa) above down to the partless (niṣkala) Śiva, who is the eternal space, the point (bindu), and the womb containing the worlds born from the vowels and the Mistress of Kalās (Kalābhuvaneśī).

I bow to Him who has Īśāna as His head, Nara as His lotus-face, Aghora as His heart, Vāma as His secret organ, and Sadyojāta as His form; whose feet are the Lord of the City (Pura), the Face, the Heart, and the State; who is the nature of the sixfold paths; whose body is fashioned from the elements, the ocean, the Siddhas, Smara, the serpents, and the Kalās; and who possesses the eyes of Action, Will, and Vision, with half a month [fifteen] as His eye—Him who resides in the Kabi-la [Kailāsa], whose body is Knowledge.

Through the union of Bhava, Hara, and Śiva with the limbs of Brahmā—manifested in the colors white, blood-red, black, yellow, crystal, moon-white, golden, crimson, and fire-colored—the form [of Śiva] appears as crystal-clear due to the identity of the mantra and its meaning. Thus, in all the Śiva-philosophies, it is declared that this is the cause of all goals; this variegated nature of the faces of the Lord of Consciousness and Unconsciousness is a wondrous manifestation.
The four faces of the Lord of All are pervaded by Īśāna, who consists of space and appears white, and whose essence is the *puruṣa*, *hṛdaya*, *guhya*, and *ajana* mantras.

Because of this, those who know Śiva understand that while this [central face] possesses a white luster, each individual face—due to the purpose of bestowing grace upon the letters residing in the eastern and other directions—is known to possess colors such as yellow and so forth.
I bow to Śiva, whose faces are Īśāna, Tatpuruṣa, Aghora, Vāmadeva, and Sadyojāta, and who assumes the forms of a child, a youth, an old man, a woman, and a man.
The Lord holds a trident and a khaṭvāṅga, possesses a spear, has a lotus in his hand, and displays the gesture of fearlessness;
he is attached to a blue lotus, a snake, and a ḍamaru drum, carries a bījapūra fruit, is beautiful, and wears a rosary.

The three powers of the All-pervasive Lord consist of consciousness, bliss, and the destruction of the fear of worldly existence; through their transformation, they manifest as the expansion of the seed of all things.

Indeed, the primordial nature (*prakṛti*), facing toward the *kalās* and other categories, is the full thread of the long eye; the mind is the collection of weapons of Śambhu. This supreme [reality] is to be known by those devoted to the Āgamas, and not the other.

I bow to Sadāśiva, the Lord of all sciences and the Sovereign of all beings, the Overlord of Brahman who, by virtue of his nature as Brahman, is eternally of undivided form. [I bow to] Mahādeva, known as Tatpuruṣa, who bestows the knowledge of Śiva upon his devotees.
I salute Rudra, the impeller of the principles (*tattva*), for the sake of attaining the state of Śiva.
Now, [I salute] the Ghoraghoratara, who is both terrible and non-terrible, and who effects the liberation from the bonds of the bound soul (*paśu*).
I bow to Śarva, the multiform one, who is the refuge for all.
I bow to Vāma, Jyeṣṭha, Raudra, Kalavikaraṇa, Balavikaraṇa, Kānta,
Balapramathana, Sarvabhūtadamana, and Manonmana.
To Sadyojāta, the omniscient one who removes the fear of worldly existence for those who bow before him;
(this half-line appears to be unmetrical āryā)

I bow to the Lord of the World, the stainless one who joins [beings] beyond existence, who arises from existence. Salutation to that Supreme One, the Great One, whose pure and stainless splendor is the Self of the universe, eternal, and the source of all majesty; he who consists of consciousness and bliss, who abides within the limit of the sky shining above through the sequential process of transcending the stations beginning with Brahmā and ending with Sadāśiva by means of the crest of the Nāda arising from the glorious Root-Mantra.

I bow to that supreme Śiva, who is partless and imperishable, whose supreme seat is measured by the moon (1), the pair (2), the qualities (3), the objects (5), their half (2.5), its quarter (1.25), sixteen (16), twenty-two (22), thirty (30), four oceans (4), sixty (60), serpents (8), ears (2), and earth (1)— that is, 1235.2516224608— and which is the state of Unmanī, reached through the rays of the fingers during the [six] Darśanas.

May Śiva protect you— he who is the first, the fifth, death, the ornament, the crescent moon, the qualities, the faith, the eye, the sun, the sound, the plow, the sun, the moon, the circle, the plowshare, the one with rays, the three-pointed flame, the two-fold reflection, the twice-bent, the Transmental (Unmanā), the All, the Beyond-all, and the Partless-all.

I bow to the Lord Prāsāda, who is partless, adorned by Śiva, Rudra, the individual soul (pudgala), and the half-moon; who possesses the four powers of Rodha, Daṇḍa, Taddanta, and Śakti; who is the master of the yogins; who is Śaṅkara, moving through eight oceans of finger-breadths; who resides in the six flavors and the void; the lord of all mantras, who traverses the six paths.

O Maheśa, the fruit of one’s birth is the worship of You through the supreme mudrās—which consist of the vision of the abiding state of consciousness and the restraint [of the senses]—and through the single-minded devotion to Śiva within one’s own limbs, as well as by the offering of water for the feet, the arghya, and flowers. Invoking [the deity] is the manifestation of consciousness within one’s own self; its stabilization therein is the installation (*sthāpana*) of the Lord.
"Sānnidhya" is the proximity of the Lord of the Self; "saṃrodhana" is one's own absorption into Śiva.
Homage be to Bhava, whose heart is perfect knowledge; homage to the one whose form is distinguished by qualities and sovereignty;
homage to you whose crest-jewel is the nature of independent mastery; homage to the self that is the armor of splendor.
Homage to the trident-bearer, whose majesty endures alongside the impurities of living beings and who wields the weapon of patience;
homage to Sadāśiva, the changeless one, whose form consists of the six limbs and who is the embodiment of nectar.
For the sake of my own purification, I perform the ritual rinsing of the feet of Śiva, who is pure by his very nature.
The offering of the *arghya* and the presentation of flowers are for the purpose of attaining the abode of the Lord of the Place (*sadeśadhāman*).

Bathing that removes the impurities of one's own self, anointing with auspicious fragrances, [offering] fine garments and ornaments, worship with fragrant flowers and garlands, the ritual offering of incense to Sadāśiva adorned with ornaments, and indeed, for the sake of the individual soul’s enjoyment in the abode of the Lord of the Place, the pure lamp which bestows the knowledge of Śiva—[all these constitute the ritual]. JsSpst_39–40*
[He should visualize] those stationed in the directions of Śuci, Īśa, Rakta, Pānīndra, Mṛtyu, and Indu— resembling clouds, the sun, wind, and fire, and possessing twelve eyes.

Salutation to those whose hands hold the boon-granting gesture, the gesture of fearlessness, the trident, and the spear; who have faces on their arms; who are born from the limbs of Śiva; and whose forms consist of the mantras beginning with the Heart-mantra.

The worship of the limbs of one’s own body as the limbs of Bhoga (the Lord) is for the sake of attaining the qualities of Śiva; furthermore, the worship of the limbs of the Lord is for the sake of the union with Śiva of the pure-souled worshipper.

The offering of food, water, mouth-fresheners, and so forth to the satisfied [deity] is for the sake of satisfying the mind; therein, the fruit of the ritual image-worship is the wonderful, auspicious state of being Śiva.
The gift of a purifier to one who has become purified destroys the threefold suffering and leads to the accomplishment of all goals;
likewise, recitation with devotion and prostration to Śiva are the cause for attaining the status of Brahmā, Indra, Viṣṇu, and others.

He who knows Hara—the Supreme Śiva—as the Arcane (arcana), as the manifest (sakala), as the one with parts and yet partless (sakalākala), as eternally arisen, as the partless (niṣkala) who traverses all paths, as the perfect one in the offering of the self; as one with the luster of clear crystal in the sky and endowed with the creative powers (kalās) in the abode—he is indeed Śiva himself, O Astra, there is no doubt.

Furthermore, worship brings about the presence of the Lord; prayer is for the sake of mutual beholding between one’s own self and the Lord; in this world, [worship] leads to enjoyment in the realm of Sadāśiva;

the offering of worship to Īśa and Agni is for the purpose of exhausting the three bonds of karma; and the surrender of one's own self to the Supreme Śiva is for the sake of the soul’s very abiding [in its true state].
The *parāṅmukha-arghya* (the oblation turned away) of the Supreme Lord is for the purpose of casting out the flood of impure principles;
by performing the emission (*visarga*) that causes [the soul] to abide in that [oblation], one attains the state of Śiva.

The eminent and lofty scholar from the Chola country, Jñānaśambhu, who was a knower of the Siddhānta, composed this pure hymn of praise for the worship of Śambhu out of devotion, according to the word of Śiva, for the sake of both worldly enjoyment and liberation.
